utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. May I introduce Ms. Emma Vasta-Kuby, who has been with my team for six weeks. She's a final-year student at Wesleyan University dealing with political science and international relations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, before we begin. I just on re-reading the transcript last night I would like to withdraw my objection to having 1D9291 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. It's noted. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pasic, following up on that same subject in answering questions during the cross-examination, you said -- you said that chaos started even before the war. I'm not going to deal with 1991. I would like to ask you about the events that happened on the eve of the war. What did you mean when you said that was there shooting. What did you have in mind when you said that chaos reigned supreme even before the war?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I meant the events which happened in the neighbouring State of Croatia, those events that happened before the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We are a municipality on the border with Croatia. We experienced civilian casualties as well in the territory of Kostunica which is what I emphasised. This is what I meant when I said there were disturbances. The fact is that from that area in one way or another illegally people crossed the border, and they were able to bring in weapons. To a large extent that aggravated the situation, and it was much more difficult to establish law and order and the functioning of local authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the position of the Serbian community in Bosanski Novo with regard to the referendum and was the referendum of the Muslim and Croatian part of Bosnia peaceful since you were a majority Serbian municipality and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm just wondering how this is relevant to the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a critical moment, and Mr. Pasic was answering the Prosecutor's questions and he painted the situation in Bosanski Novi. The referendum was a very critical moment so I would like Mr. Pasic to tell us how the authorities managed to maintain peace longer than other places in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The question was how this line of questioning arises out of the cross-examination of Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because Mr. Pasic's words were doubted when he said that the authorities had major problems in managing the crisis, so I wanted the Trial Chamber to see what was happening on the eve of the war, even in Sarajevo, at the end of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think -- I can -- I think you can fairly move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Do you want to still add to anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just as a slight reminder and admonition. I also looked up the representation that Dr. Karadzic made about what the witness ostensibly said, and it's not reflected in yesterday's transcript. Therefore, it represents Dr. Karadzic attempting to feed the witness information that he wants him to affirm, and that was another aspect of the need to be addressed. So I didn't think the Court or anyone else had an opportunity to actually peruse the transcript, and having done so that's the result. Dr. Karadzic who has been reminded about this repeatedly needs to refrain from leading commentary in his -- in the questions he poses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Shall we continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm sure that the following question will arise from the Prosecutor's questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, how did the bodies of authorities, primarily police, treat perpetrators of crime? Did Muslims return? Were there any criminal activities by the Serbs and by the Muslims, and how did the police treat those?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to point out that during those difficult times there were certain crimes including stealing or killings. The public security station worked within its purview as much as it could. Let me give you some examples, and we've already talked about that. The police, which was under the control of the Serbian authorities, did not make a distinction between a criminal of Serbian ethnicity or of other ethnicities. For example, a killing, a murder took place at the beginning of June. A Muslim was killed, and the public security station arrested the perpetrator within the next three days. He was a Serb. This means that our organs worked as much as they could. The perpetrators were processed. Don't ask me, because I don't know to what sentence was given to that person, but he was a Serb, and as a Serb he was convicted and sentenced because of the aggravated murder that he committed. He killed a Muslim, and that Serbian -- Serb went on trial, and he was convicted. There were also examples when Muslim property was stolen by Serb perpetrators. Court proceedings were instituted against them. Those people were convicted and sentenced for stealing property. There is also an example where a person of Serb ethnicity -- or, rather, there were people of Serb ethnicity in paramilitary formations. They put up resistance at a check-point which was manned by the policemen from the SJB. They tried to carry out some illegal activities. The police reacted. They had to use weapons, and that Serb, that one Serb who was a member of a paramilitary unit was killed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 1D4828. Does this mean that there's no translation? I was hoping that there would be translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There is no translation, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In that case could you please tell us who issued this document, and what did the police in Bosanski Novi do in that respect?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who issued the document?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can it be zoomed in, please? CSB sector SMB Banja Luka, Operative Boro Bukva. This could have been somebody from the police. I don't know from which department.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: National security.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that it was the National Security Service. This person Boro Bukva was its employee. I believe that he's the one who drafted this document. This person does hail from the municipality of Bosanski Grad, Bosanski Novi, if there is nobody else under that same name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us about the contents of this document? Did the disarming start? What about criminal procedure? I'm particularly interested in the penultimate paragraph to see who those people were who threatened. Can the page be scrolled up a little. There was a group of five people who were processed. Were they Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just take a moment and find them. Where is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Penultimate.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Participated --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, without a transcript I'm strapped as to making any objections as to this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you ask the witness to read out the paragraph in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, could you please slowly read.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is underlined in red?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First the bigger paragraph and then the smaller or the shorter paragraph. Can you do it aloud?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Performed an interview with people who were --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This is impossible to translate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, could you read out again, this time very slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "He carried out interviews with people who were arrested and who belonged to sabotage terrorist groups (the first group 8 armed persons of Muslim ethnicity which had been set up in the territory of Prijedor-Puharska, was moving across" -- I believe it says -- that it says "Kureva" here "and the territory of Ljubija. It was spotted and --"

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is incidents in Prijedor if we're talking about Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, the entire chapter is about Bosanski Novi. Those are two neighbouring municipalities. So that village is possibly closer to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Ljubija borders on one part of Novi Grad municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And it says here that the group was neutralised in the territory --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you read the last --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's impossible to follow if you overlap each other. I don't know why this is relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, your Excellency, if he had written -- read the whole sentence it would have been clear. The group was set up in the area of Bosanski Novi. It is originally from Ljubija, but it was neutralised in Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we hear the paragraph in its entirety first. Could you read from where you stopped.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "... was neutralised in the area of Bosanski Novi. The purpose was to tie up with the forces from Cazin Krajina. The second group, 18 armed individuals, was set up in the area of Bosanski Novi where it was neutralised. Fifteen individuals were arrested, and two of their associates. The purpose of the movement of the said group was to cross over to the territory of the Cazin Krajina." The other paragraph that is encircled: "He participated along with SJB from Bos Novi in the processing of five individual group from Bosanski Novi who by committing acts, endangering general public and thereby threatened the physical and property security of citizens."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just a second. Now, was your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, can you tell us with respect to these two paragraphs, who were the perpetrators in the first one and who in the one beneath?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood it correctly, we are talking here about two groups that were crossing the territory of Bosanski Novi. The first group was made up of Muslims who were coming from the direction of Prijedor via Novi towards the Cazin Krajina. The second group was made up of Muslims from Bosanski Novi or Novi Grad municipality who were also apprehended in the area with the same objective in mind, which was to establish contact with the Muslims of the Cazin Krajina. In this bottom paragraph, as I understand it, the operative in question processed a group of five individuals from Bosanski Novi. In view of the paragraph above, it only makes sense that the five individuals were also Muslims but from the other group mentioned above, that was made up of 18 individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, again I question the relevance of this information relating to the cross-examination of Mr. Pasic yesterday. The document's dated the 13th of October, 1992, clearly months and months after the incidents that we were discussing yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I precisely selected this document which demonstrates that there was no peace in Novi Grad or Bosanski Novi municipality for months before the events that were described. There had been permanent danger lurking there, and we can see that even Serbs were being apprehended. There were groups who were passing across the territory whose aspiration was to create chaos and fighting. On page 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are not giving evidence. Ms. Sutherland indicated this is related to events months after what she discussed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is one and the same event, a prolonged event that the essence -- you can see that on page 3. There is a paragraph which describes what they encountered, and we can see whether the authorities did the best they could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us see how it is relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see the last page --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. He is just asking Mr. Pasic to read the document. He is not actually asking him any questions to which [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think he laid some foundational questions, so let's see whether it's related to his question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please read this paragraph, and then I'm going to ask you a question, the one marked red.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "According to the available intelligence, a number of Muslim emigres (from Bosanski Novi) is carrying out hostile actions, particularly in the area of the Republic of Croatia and are preparing themselves for sabotage and terrorist activities in the area of Republika Srpska."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us how long did the war last in your municipality, bearing in mind what you said about 1991? Were the authorities in any way in position to face a normal situation?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Novi Grad or Bosanski Novi municipality, one can say that the war started sometime in June of 1991 and that it ended only after the signing of the Dayton Accords in 1995. So this entire period was marked by a difficult situation. Of course, there were on and off rises and decreases of danger, but throughout the period there was an imminent threat of war in Novi Grad, Bosanski Novi municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, the people mentioned in this paragraph who were from Bosanski Novi and who were let go to Croatia, how did they return, in what capacity?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they mainly returned across combat lines. They were all armed and wearing uniforms. They were coming in specific military formation or units. There were even some details recorded to the effect that there was fierce fighting in the area of Suva Medja, which is the area dividing the municipality of Novi Grad and Bosanska Krupa facing Cazim Gujim [phoen]. This is the area where these people were already dressed in uniforms. They were members of the military. They were under the leadership of Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were amongst them --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat the question from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is concerning the citizens of Bosanski Novi. Were amongst them those who you allowed to go to Banja Luka -- to Croatia instead of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will give you a specific example: The gentleman who was conducting negotiations on the bridge, and he was a member of the Muslim delegation named Nedim Muftic - we mentioned him yesterday - when he was talking to the commissioner for refugees, according to what I know, was killed as a soldier of the BH Army of Alija Izetbegovic precisely in the battle-field that I mentioned, and that is the one between Bosanska Krupa and Novi Grad. In other words, he was killed as a soldier, whereas he had left as a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were amongst them individuals who were held at the Mlakve stadium? I'm talking about able-bodied men.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Most of them were persons fit for military service. The great majority of them left as civilians, but once they reached the territory of Croatia, they were then sent back to Central Bosnia where they were trained to fight, and they were mobilised and eventually took part as members of the BH Army. I cannot say that this pertains to all of them, but we have information that there were many of them among those ranks.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted and MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can handle that because I had a chance while Ms. Sutherland was actually listening to the evidence to scroll back and look at what the witness said about the document. He was asked: Can you tell us anything about the contents. He was then directed to a particular paragraph, and then it's very clear from the record that he was only parsing out the -- what he could glean from what he had just read from the document. If I understood it correctly, we're talking here about, and then he compared one paragraph to another. He had no independent information to provide about this document, no contextualisation. So his evidence stands on its on own but it doesn't require the document in any way to assist it, and I don't think directing a witness to a document and asking him to read it and explain what it is he thinks he's reading has been a basis for admission in our courtroom thus far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The foundational question Mr. Karadzic put to the witness before he put this document to the witness was this: "How did the bodies of authorities, primarily police, treat perpetrators of crime? Did Muslims return? Were there any criminal activities by the Serbs and by the Muslims, and how did the police treat those?" And the document had nothing to do with those questions, and I'm not quite sure how this is relevant to or arose out of the cross-examination of Ms. Sutherland. Can you help us, Mr. Robinson or Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will gladly do so. The persons who returned were originally allowed to go to Croatia, not to Banja Luka as had been offered by the authorities. The authorities offered them to go to the deep part of the Serbian territory. Instead, they went to Croatia, and they returned as soldiers. Those were not simply civilians. Those were civilians fit for military service. The people who did not want to go to Banja Luka, they wanted to go to Croatia, were held at the Mlakve stadium. We heard that the representative who -- of the UNHCR who talked alone with them, they told him that they wanted to go to Croatia instead of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber -- the Chamber does not consider this document relevant. We'll not admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I'm going to show only one document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A minute ago you said that the Serb perpetrators of crimes committed against Muslims was also arrested and prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see one document on the ELMO. I have the translation, but I misplaced it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have a 65 ter number, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll find it in a minute. I was looking in the wrong place. ERN number is 03085987. That's 1D9166, but it's not in e-court since I hadn't anticipated that we would need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this name, and are you familiar with the names of the victims below? Do you remember this incident?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the names. I know some of them. I know the name of this Serb called Milanko Vujanovic. I'm not personally acquainted with the Muslim victims who were listed below.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, on what basis? What witness told us is the name of the -- a certain Vujanovic and the fact that there are some Muslim victims. What is it about, and how is it relevant, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said in cross-examination that the authorities treated the perpetrators equally regardless of their ethnicity. In this case, the perpetrator is a Serb, and the victims are Muslims. And there was no discrimination against --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You need to lead the witness -- ask the question what crime you are talking about at least. We heard nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, a while ago, as well as yesterday, you said that the authorities did not discriminate against the perpetrators on ethnic basis. Can you tell us the ethnicity of the perpetrator and that of the victims?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Everything that was discovered through gathering intelligence that confirmed that a crime was committed, the public security station and the judiciary treated such incidents regardless of the fact of who the perpetrators were. In this particular instance that I'm looking at involves Milenko Vujanovic, who was a Serb, and I'm familiar with that name. I know that he was being tried, that he was convicted for the crime committed against the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, it was homicide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Sutherland, any objection to the admission of this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: To this criminal report, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Well' receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3851, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Excellencies, I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wish to further re-examine the witness, please, on one point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: About what, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's in relation to the answer he gave on page 4, lines 1 to 19. It's about this very issue of people being convicted. Mr. Karadzic asked the witness about a certain incident, and I want to put something to the witness about that and show him a document, because otherwise you have a skewed view of the reality of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, you remember -- you remember a moment ago you'd pointed out an example of a killing, a murder that took place at the beginning of June, a Muslim was killed. Are you referring to Husein Hotic? And the perpetrators being Goran Pekic and Zoran Djukic, and Mladen Djukic and Goran Djukic? Is that the incident that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you said they were convicted and sentenced because of the aggravated murder that -- that was committed? They went on trial and they were convicted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can have 65 ter 25357, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, we can see when the document comes on the screen that this -- the trial didn't occur until 2007, and they were actually convicted at that point. So there was nothing done by the Bosanski Novi municipality judiciary throughout the conflict in relation to this person being tried and sentenced and convicted and sentenced; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. It is simply unbelievable that you as a member of the legal profession should not distinguish between the various jurisdictions. You should not know that there are prosecution offices and courts, that there should be law enforcement agencies, prosecutors offices and courts as three different structures. I can tell you with full responsibility that the public security station responded in a timely manner, apprehended the perpetrators, and that was the remit within which they were able to act. It's not fair you asking me about when the conviction was rendered since our judiciary bodies are independent from the legislative and executive branches. Now what the reasons were, what were the elements why a certain criminal proceeding went on for two, four, or six years, at any rate, proceedings were carried out, sentences were rendered, which means that justice was meted out to the perpetrators of the crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Pass, the way you answered this question was that it was -- it was processed immediately. I am simply showing you a document that shows that this matter was not dealt with until 15 years after the event.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was that question for the witness, your last comment? Let me put -- let me put to the witness. Mr. Pasic, in your answer you said this: "I can tell you with full responsibility that the public security station responded in a timely manner, apprehended the perpetrators ..." Do you know when these perpetrators were apprehended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't be precise and certain, but I can state with full responsibility - I think that you have it in writing somewhere - that the perpetrators of this crime were apprehended five days after the commission of the crime. In my view, in view of the fact that there was a war on, this was done within record-breaking time, since in peacetime it can take months and even years to detect the perpetrators and locate them. That's why I said that this was done within record time, within five days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was taking issue as to when the perpetrators were -- he said the perpetrators were processed and they were convicted and sentenced, and that was what I was taking issue at, was when that was occurring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you are going to ask further questions or you stopped, you concluded?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So my question would be, Mr. Pasic, we can see from the document that we have in front of us that these people were not processed, were not tried, within a reasonable amount of time and certainly not during the war. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm your hypothesis, because I didn't work as part of the justice administration with the judiciary or the prosecutors' offices. What the arguments were, what the reasoning was is a question that should be directed to the judiciary involved. It obviously is not something that you would agree with, but I was not able to exert any influence of this to have an influence over the timing or the substance of this judgement. So the question that you're putting to me is not appropriately addressed to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6441, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, Excellencies? When Ms. Sutherland finishes, I will need a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And just one other quick matter, Mr. Pasic. On page 11 at line 12, you mentioned Nedim Muftic. You were, in fact, referring to Nedim Puric, the gentleman's evidence that I read out yesterday. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. When I spoke about the negotiations taking place at the bridge over the Una River, I said that there were representatives of the Muslim ethnicity, and I will repeat their names: Emin Puric, Amir Delic, Mirsad Brkic, Nedim Muftic. There were four individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At the outset of today's hearing you said you withdrew the objection about 1D9291. Could you --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I thought that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I thought that the witness had simply read the document, but he commented in a couple of sentences after -- after reading the beginning of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, actually, I had difficulty locating that document. Could you tell us the 1D exhibit number or 65 ter number again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have no track of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's on line 25, page 41112 of yesterday's transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pasic, can you tell us this sixth or seventh line, convicted previously in 1992 by a conviction rendered by the Banja Luka High Court. Do you see that? And then it says a suspended sentence of two years, et cetera. So was it the case that there was a trial conducted in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you with certainty that I didn't read any judgements. Besides, this isn't made readily available to all the members of the public but only to those who were parties to the proceeding. So I cannot give my comment on any details of any judgement; that would not be reliable. However, I do find the names of these individuals familiar, and I know that they were convicted during the war for certain criminal offences. It would be highly inappropriate of me to say now what the sentences rendered were and precisely for which criminal offences, but these can easily be found at the Banja Luka District Court and Novi Grad District Court. Therefore, in the beginning, during the war, and after the war, all the -- all the criminal offence proceedings that were conducted are archived and can be found in these archives. Many Serbs, not just these ones, were tried for criminal offences regardless of the criminal offence involved and regardless of the ethnicities involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why was this tried before the Banja Luka court rather than the Novi Sad court in the first instance, or the Novi Grad court?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have to know that it will depend on the subject matter jurisdiction. Novi Grad comes under Banja Luka, and Banja Luka will -- the Banja Luka court will have the subject matter jurisdiction for what is committed in Novi Grad. All the criminal offences incurring sentences that -- exceeding ten years will be addressed at the Banja Luka District Court, whereas those incurring sentences fewer than ten years will be treated by the Banja Luka first instance court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have document 2016 and the Serbian page 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, do you agree that the -- that these previous convictions related to the same crime?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I don't. It's a different court, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or maybe just previous conviction on -- for other matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Karadzic, with the observation of Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I don't know what K14 is. It's a case file obviously. I don't know what he was tried for, but we can see that he was tried and we'll see when he was prosecuted by the Banja Luka prosecutor's office. So if we look at page 5, we will see when the case was processed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- even under non bis in idem he wouldn't be convicted for the same crime, so -- and it's a different court. It -- its -- it's arguably a different matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was asking whether it was a trial in absentia and now a trial with the accused in custody. Let us see page 5.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 5 in Serbian and then we'll be able to find what the page -- the corresponding page in English is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The last paragraph. Mr. Pasic, can you happen us with this? It reads: "The prosecutor's office has adduced before the court evidence in the form of the witness statement," et cetera. Page 4 in English if we can have it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me say first that we do have the non bis in idem principle in our jurisdiction. However, we also have ordinary and extraordinary legal remedies. With ordinary legal remedies there can be a retrial in case that new evidence emerges that was not previously known when initially the trial was conducted. So that is with the extraordinary legal remedies. So it can be the case that even where a case was tried should new details, new facts, arguments, or evidence emerge there can be a retrial. I'm looking at this paragraph. It says 5 July 1992. If that's what you're referring to as well, I mean the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Can you read out two sentences.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Can you just zoom in a bit: "The prosecutor's office has adduced before the court evidence in the form of witness statement --" I can't make it out. Is it Starcevic, the family name?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be zoomed in, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please. "The prosecutor's office has adduced before the Court evidence in the form of witness statement given by Stevo Starcevic before an investigating judge on 5 July 1992 about this particular incident in case Ki 33/92 with which the court in Bosanski Novi is seized. Furthermore, the prosecutor's office has provided official notes of interviews of these witnesses."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you just read out where it says that on 3 July 1992 a passenger car was seized from the accused Goran Petic. Can you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we see here that this was the Zastava 101 vehicle complete with the vehicle licence at which point a receipt or certificate was drawn up where the vehicle was returned to owner of Emir Veletanlic who is a Muslim and the other person is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we see when --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the accused please repeat his question. It is very difficult to work like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic. The interpreters were not able to hear your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us when was it that Husein Hotic was declared dead? He was the victim of this criminal event.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises. We cannot interpret if we do not have the translation on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters find it very difficult to follow without the relevant passage before them, but it's up to you how to spend your time, but, Mr. Karadzic, this is admitted, and everything is in evidence. I don't see the point of going through with the witness about this point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I've achieved what I wanted to achieve.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I would like know whether the authorities in Bosanski Novi accomplished everything and did the courts --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- and the police allow for the state of lawlessness to reign?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, how does that further re-examination arise out of my cross-examination on that one particular document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you not ask the witness that it was until -- it was not until 2007 that it was processed?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No. I said in relation to the -- it going to trial it wasn't processed until 2007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now, this question was about authorities in Bosanski Novi, which may include the judiciary or -- et cetera. Mr. Robinson, could you help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm torn between thinking what a colossal waste of time some of this is and the actual question of whether it arises. I think that it does arise out of the redirect -- or re-cross-examination, because the allegation was made that they did nothing during this period, and that's why it wasn't until 2007 that this was brought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm really wondering whether we should spend time on this. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, because this implicates something we do over and over again, the direct examination, cross-examination, redirect examination, re-cross-examination is in virtually every courtroom a very narrowing process, and the question raised was about a particular matter raised by Dr. Karadzic in respect of a particular document which is the reason why you permitted the re-cross. It's not because that very, very narrow issue obviously implicates in some manner the broader issues of the case, does not make it a matter of opening the door to that very broad issue. We were narrowing this thing down to the one matter about the document. Again, like Mr. Robinson, I'm not concerned about this particular issue. If Dr. Karadzic chooses to waste more time in -- as he wishes, I guess that's his prerogative, but I think we do need to follow the normal practice in respect of examinations, and that is the focus is on a particular matter. The fact that that particular matter implicates the broader issues of the case doesn't mean now we can now go back to square one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. No, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees with Mr. Tieger. Unless you have anything further, we'll conclude the evidence of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Unless my colleagues have a question for you, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Pasic. I thank you for coming to The Hague to give it. Now you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it the next witness is ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The next witness is Zvonko Bajagic, and before he is brought in, if we could just go to private session for one moment while we deal with an exhibit from another witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it Bajagic or Bajajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Bajagic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm wondering whether we need a hearing tomorrow at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think we will if we are efficient today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness -- headphones, please. Yes. Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you. May Godspeed be with you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bajagic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. The President of the Trial Chamber, may I ask you to allow me to say just one sentence that you never heard or that you will never hear in your whole life, and I'm sure that it will find a place in your heart. I've always uttered that one sentence about those important days and those important events. It's going to be a very brief sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic will ask you questions if necessary and if they are relevant. I'm not sure what you have in mind, but let us proceed. I was told that you were not feeling well yesterday, but during the course of today's testimony if you do not feel well, please don't hesitate to let us know, Mr. Bajagic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm as good as new now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Bajagic.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: May God help you and may you have all the good luck in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please make a pause after my question. I will make a pause after your answer. And could you please speak slowly and use the fewest possible number of words in order to work efficiently today. Mr. Bajagic, did you provide a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D090151 in e-court. No, no. 1D09151. That's the correct number. There is no extra zero in that number. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at the screen, look at the left-hand side of the screen, Mr. Bajagic. Is this the statement that you provided?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: On the left-hand side? There are two screens here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look on the left. It will be the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: No. There is no such thing. There is just the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On my screen it's on the left.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Oh, you mean this screen. I've told you I had two screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you read the statement, and did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown the last page to identify the signature on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Mr. President. This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the statement accurately reflect what you stated before the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's a true and accurate reflection of what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today, would your answers be the same in essence?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: They would be, Mr. President. They would be the same, and there would be some additional clarifications, because the -- we have shortened the whole thing, and there are so many other important things to be said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can be statement be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Welcome back, Mr. Mitchell. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3853, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'm going to read a short summary of Mr. Zvonko Bajagic's statement in English. [In English] Zvonko Bajagic was a private entrepreneur before the war. Before the war he was president of the church board in Vlasenica. He met President Radovan Karadzic after Dr. Karadzic was elected president of the SDS party. They -- they shared a common heritage, and their ancestors were from the Niksic area. During the years, Mr. Bajagic visited President Karadzic in his office in Pale and saw him at other locations within Republika Srpska. Mr. Bajagic was one of the organisers of a mass funeral in Vlasenica on 30th of September, 1992. While he does not recall the details of President Karadzic's speech, he recalls that people in the audience thought he was too conciliatory towards the Muslims. Mr. Bajagic knew President Karadzic to be against any acts against Muslim civilians and always sought to reduce tensions. President Karadzic asked Mr. Bajagic to use his authority in the Vlasenica area to protect Muslim civilians. In July 1995, after the fall of Srebrenica, Mr. Bajagic went to the office of President Karadzic one day. According to the appointment book of President Karadzic, that was in the late evening of 14th of July, 1995. Mr. Bajagic encountered President Karadzic only briefly and observed that President Karadzic was angry about something. During his time in President Karadzic's cabinet, he never heard of any information that prisoners from Srebrenica had been, were being, or would be killed. Knowing President Karadzic as he did, Mr. Bajagic is sure that President Karadzic would never be in favour or condone any killings of prisoners. [Interpretation] Thank you. At this moment I have no further questions for the gentleman, but I would like to allow Mr. Karadzic [as interpreted] to tell us what he offered to tell us, and may that be part of the examination-in-chief. He wanted to utter a sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a sentence that I would like to utter because this is a very big day in my life, because I am in the centre of the world of justice. Mr. President, I'm sure that you yourself have not heard this sentence. That is why I would like to utter that sentence. It's a simple sentence. The true Lord support us with the force of your holy spirit. Let me not testify falsely. Avert a false word from my tongue. Glory to you, Lord.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now I hand the witness over to the Prosecutor -- Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the record, on this page, line 11, "to allow Mr. Karadzic" should read "to allow Mr. Bajagic." Yes, Mr. Bajagic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing, that is, through your written witness statement in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Mr. President of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, this morning you said at page 29 of our transcript, line 25, that your statement had been shortened and that there were some important things to be said. Can I have your statement -- sorry, your statement is in e-court. Can we go to page 5 in English, page 6 in the B/C/S. And if you can just concentrate on paragraph 35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You may refer to the hard copy, Mr. Bajagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bajagic, you said there were some other important things to be said. I want to ask you about three important things that you did on the 13th of July that aren't in this particular paragraph of your statement about what you did on 13 July. Now, the first important thing that isn't in your statement is that you were at the football field in Nova Kasaba on the afternoon of 13 July 1995, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: This is not correct. I was not at the football pitch. I just passed along the road, and the football pitch was on the left-hand side. It's a main road, and whoever passed along that road could see that the football pitch was there. I myself was not in the football pitch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. But you stopped at the football pitch, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did stop there just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And when you say "we," you're talking about you and two group volunteers who were in your car; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. We stopped there just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, there were a lot of captured Muslims sitting on the football field at the time, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. And the two group volunteers who were with you, they were there to assist in the Srebrenica operation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: But they were in your car and you were on your way to Srebrenica; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, you asked me a question about those two volunteers. Those two volunteers were not there to help with the operation in Srebrenica. They just kept me company. We were on our way to Srebrenica. We were curious to see that Srebrenica at the hand of whose inhabitants we suffered greatly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: But they were soldiers, weren't they? They were attached to the Vlasenica Brigade.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: They were soldiers, volunteers, attached to the Vlasenica Brigade. They were Greeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: All right. Now, one of these volunteers had a camera, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. One of them had a camera but not a film camera, a still-photo camera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And he took two or three photos of those prisoners, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. He got out of the car and he took photos of those people who were in the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic [Realtime transcript read in error "Poparic"] was at the Nova Kasaba football field then, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: He was on the main road. He was standing right in front of our vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic was the assistant commander for security in your unit, right, in the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And so Mr. Popovic saw this Greek volunteer taking photos of the prisoners, and he came over and asked him what he was doing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And then Popovic confiscated the camera with those photos of the prisoners on it.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question? I did not understand it the first time around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Certainly. Mr. Popovic saw the Greek volunteer taking photos of the prisoners, and he came over and confiscated that camera from the Greek volunteer; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: No, he did not confiscate it. He just drew my attention to the fact that that should not be done, that photos should not be taken and that we should give him that camera or that the film should be taken out and exposed to light so that the photos would be lost, but I told him, Popovic, I give you my guarantee that those photos will never be seen by anybody or that they will be reproduced, so there's no need for you to confiscate that camera from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And did you make sure that those photos were exposed and would never be seen by anybody?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I have never seen them, never so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, and if I can just make a couple of transcript corrections. I think the last page repeatedly referred to Lieutenant-Colonel "Poparic." It should be "Popovic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It should be Popovic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Just one more question about Nova Kasaba. Did you see General Mladic at Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him. He wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: No, he wasn't there. I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: What about Milomir Savcic, the commander of the 65th Protection Regiment?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Milomir Savcic wasn't there either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can -- I'm about to move to a different area, so this might be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Before we break, you referred to the Drina Corps as his unit. Could you clarify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, you were a member of the Drina Corps, were you not, the Logistics Battalion of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: The Drina Corps did not have a Logistics Battalion, and I was a desk officer for logistics. That was my duty. That was my position, but you don't need a battalion for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. But you were a desk officer for logistics for the Drina Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. You may put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, just before the break I asked you whether Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic confiscated the camera from the Greek volunteer, and you said no he didn't confiscate it. I just want to clarify. Is it your testimony that he did or he didn't confiscate that camera?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I first said that it was not a camera. It was an ordinary photo camera. Then I said that he did not confiscate it. That's what I said in my answer a while ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You testified in the state court in the case of Franc Kos on the 4th of November, 2011, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you'd agree that two years ago your memory of this incident would have been fresher; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: You have to remind me better. Fresher in what sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Why don't I just read to you what you said in the Kos case. You were asked -- you mentioned Colonel Popovic being there, and then you were asked: "Are you talking about Vujadin Popovic?" And your answer was: "Yes. And Vujadin asked him," talking about the Greek volunteer, "What are you taking pictures of? What are you doing? Something like that. Let me take the camera off of you. And so he took it, the camera, so we," and there's an indiscernible word, "to vehicle and left for Srebrenica." So in the Kos case you said Vujadin Popovic did take the camera.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Thank you for reminding me. I suppose that he only took it, opened it, and exposed the film to light. I suppose that that's what might have happened. Now, Mr. Prosecutor, that was a long time ago. One cannot remember every single full stop or comma or anything else after such a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So to be absolutely clear, you gave Vujadin Popovic your guarantee that these photos would never be seen by anybody, they would never be reproduced, and Popovic still wasn't happy with that, and so he took the camera and exposed the photos there and then himself; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, you're saying that he took the photo and exposed the film. That's what you are saying. A while ago I stated that I suppose that he may have taken it and exposed the film. That's all. Hopefully you are satisfied with this answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I think I'll move on. I think that's clear. Now, Mr. Bajagic, you were in your VRS Golf at the time, weren't you, your car?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I have 65 ter 25352 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: What you're about to see, Mr. Bajagic, is a document from the 20th of November, 1992. It's assigning a vehicle to you for the needs of military post 7111. Post 7111 is the Drina Corps, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And we can see at the top in the first -- the very first paragraph it says that you're being given this vehicle in order to ensure preconditions for the implementation of official tasks. So this was a car that you used for official things; right? You didn't use it for personal trips.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: It depended. Sometimes I used it for my personal needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You used a VRS army car that was given to you for official -- official tasks sometimes for your personal use. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. And we can see there the registration number of the car, P7105. It's the same car that you had throughout the war; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, I did drive other vehicles as well depending on what task I had to go to accomplish, decided what the car I would use, and also some of the vehicles were broken, and then one had to use a different vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, we'll come back to the issue of your car later. Now, I want to ask you about -- just very briefly you remember testifying in the Popovic case in 2009; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember testifying, but I cannot remember the details. If you need anything specific, could you kindly remind me if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You understood in that case that Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic was on trial for the murder of those prisoners, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, can we have the reference that it says that this relates specifically to those prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor in line 10 said that he was convicted for the murder of those prisoners who had been seen in Kasaba. Are we talking about the Kasaba prisoners, and is there any reference pointing to them being the prisoners in Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I think the judgement makes that very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we can continue. Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, it's very simple, Mr. Bajagic. You didn't mention going to Nova Kasaba or seeing the prisoners or seeing Lieutenant Popovic either confiscate this camera or confiscate it and expose the film. You didn't mention this incident at all in that case, did you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to the second big important thing about your movement on 13 July that isn't in your statement in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If I can play Exhibit P4201, the Srebrenica trial video. And, Your Honours, if you have the hard copy book, the transcript of this is at page 04077886.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is too dark. I can't discern anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we adjust the angle with the assistance of our usher. Let us see whether you can see better. Do you hear the sound, Mr. Bajagic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I was told that ... Mr. Bajagic, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. USHER
utterances.text: He can here you, but he cannot hear the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm told that there's a problem with the e-court. We need to rise for five minutes to fix it. --- Break taken at 11.16 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, we'd moved on to the second important thing that was missing from your statement --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear you. What did you say? Was it about your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. My last name is Bajagic, not Bajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'll do my best to pronounce it properly, Mr. Bajagic. I wanted to ask you about another important thing, the second important thing that's missing from your statement in relation to 13 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can play P4201, part 3 of the Srebrenica trial video starting at 1 minute and 39 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Mladic: Are you from here? "Woman: Yes, I am, from this house. "Mladic: From this house? "Woman: Yes. "Mladic: When were you expelled from here? "Woman: On 10 April 1992. "Mladic: Is there anything inside? Have you been inside? "Woman: Yes, I have. "Mladic: Well, here you are. Let's go in. "This is your own house? "Woman: It's my own house. "Mladic: They have destroyed all of this? "Woman: All of it. I just got in through the gate. "Mladic: Did you have any children? "Woman: I have two, two children, a daughter and a son. "Mladic: What about your husband? "Woman: My husband was here with my mother-in-law. When the roads were closed off, he left and was killed right at the beginning of the war. "Mladic: He was killed? "Woman: Yes. "Mladic: Do you know who killed him? "Woman: I don't know. "Mladic: And do you know where he was buried? "Woman: I don't know that either. "Mladic: What kind of work" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Pause there. And that's at 2 minutes and 31 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, can you identify for us on the right-hand side of the screen close to the camera, that's General Mladic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. You can see that it's General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And moving across to the left, the second person, that's you; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: No. This is too dark. You can't see that. You can only see Mladic here. Nothing can be seen in the background.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, look harder, Mr. Bajagic. That's you, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You may come closer to the monitor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm looking into the screen, but I can see nothing. I can only see Mladic and the woman. I can't make out these contours in the background.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: That was the same --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's dark.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: That was same in the video, but in the e-court is a little bit better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have a printout?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'm just looking for it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you ask whether you -- whether he was there with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, you heard the President's question. You were there in Srebrenica with General Mladic, weren't you, on 13 July?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. We met.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Right. And if I can get you to continue across, to skip the next gentleman, the third in, the fourth one whose head you can just see over the top of the woman, that's Colonel Petar Salapura, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I can only clearly see Mladic. It's dark and you can't make out these figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, maybe we can bring up Exhibit P4202, e-court page 115. It's page 115. We can blow the photo right up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. The person with the number 3 on their chest, that's you, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: If you could lighten it up a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, why don't we -- why don't I ask you about the person with a number 2 next to his head. That's very light. That's Colonel Salapura, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: That's what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, are you --

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Now you can see it. Yes. Now you can tell it's Salapura.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see myself now as well. I can see now that I was here as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Colonel Salapura is the -- or was the chief of the VRS Main Staff intelligence organ, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you were aware at the time, were you not, that Colonel Salapura had professional control over the 10th Sabotage Detachment?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you to repeat the first part of your question? I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I was asking if you were aware at the time of this meeting that Colonel Salapura and General Mladic, that Colonel Salapura had professional control of the 10th Sabotage Detachment.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Please, once more. You mentioned a meeting. Can you please define your question reasonably. A moment ago you didn't mention a meeting. The word used was "meeting."

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, let me stop you there. The question is simple. On the 13th of July, 1995, did you know that Colonel Salapura had professional control over the 10th Sabotage Detachment?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. You see, now you were clear. Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Right. Let's move to the third important thing that's not in your statement in relation to 13 July. In the late afternoon hours of that day, General Mladic came to your house, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Which date did you say, sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Same day as this, 13 July.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And he sat out on the terrace and had a beer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So you're sitting -- sitting out on the terrace with General Mladic having a beer, and the chief of the Vlasenica police, Milenko Majstorovic came by your house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And Milenko Majstorovic said Tomo Kovac, the deputy minister of the interior, was either at the police station or the corps in Vlasenica, at the Drina Corps headquarters in Vlasenica; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I think that he said that he may have been in the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, maybe I can remind you of what you said in the Kos case in 2011. This is page 12 of the Kos transcript, and you said: "The chief of the police, he came by and he said, 'Tomo is either in the police or the corps.'" So does that remind you of where Tomo Kovac was at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Look, you refreshed my memory somewhat now. I'm rewinding this film, trying to recall some other details. I do remember that chief of police Milenko Majstorovic told General Mladic when he got there that Tomo Kovac was in Vlasenica, either at the police station, the corps, or the hotel. He added the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So General Mladic asked you to go and find Tomo Kovac, right, and to check where he was?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So you went and found him. You went and found Tomo Kovac.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And where did you --

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I found him but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- find him?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, that I can't remember. I did find him, but I don't know where. I'm not sure, but I did find him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And after you found him, General Mladic and Tomo Kovac had a meeting, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: General Mladic sent me to find him and call him to my house. The reason was that they should discuss something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, you were at this meeting, weren't you, Mr. Bajagic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, in my mind this wasn't a meeting. It was a short encounter. They discussed something, but out of courtesy I didn't want to sit at the table with them. I assumed that as two commanders, commander of the Serbian Army and the commander of the Serbian police, had something to talk about. So I went out while the two of them had a word. What they talked about, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bajagic, it's our case that the commander of the VRS Main Staff and the deputy minister of the interior definitely had something to talk about on the afternoon of 13 July. This is our case on what that meeting was about. Tomo Kovac came to Vlasenica from Pale. He had been in a meeting with President Karadzic that ended at 4.10 p.m., that's in President Karadzic's appointment diary P2242. So Tomo Kovac then comes to Vlasenica and meets General Mladic in the late afternoon hours of 13 July right around the time of the Kravica warehouse execution is starting. So given the timing, the location and the participants of this meeting, it had to be about the Srebrenica prisoners; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: That's what you say. How should I know what they talked about? I said a moment ago that I was not present during their discussion. I courteously offered them coffee and drinks as a host, let them to discuss the matter, and then when they ended their conversation, I came back to offer some other hospitality.
