I have no way of knowing what they were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, we've talked about three things, three important things, that weren't in your statement in this case, your visit at Nova Kasaba, seeing the prisoners there, your being with General Mladic and Colonel Salapura in Srebrenica. And this meeting between the commander of the VRS Main Staff and the deputy minister of the interior. Mr. Bajagic, you left them out of that statement, didn't you, because you didn't want the Trial Chamber to know when you went up to meet the president in the early hours of the 15th of July who you'd been meeting with and the fact that you knew about prisoners at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Firstly, I'd like to ask you to split this long question in two or three and then I'll answer it. You've put ten questions in one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, I'll simplify it for you. We have talked about three things this morning that were not in your statement in this case, and the reason that they're not in your statement is because you didn't want the Trial Chamber to know who you'd been meeting with and that you knew about prisoners when you went up to meet with him on the late night of 14 July; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Hold right there. Again, three questions in one sentence. Let's take things one at a time. I apologise, Mr. Prosecutor. I asked you to split the question in two or three and take things one at a time and then I will be able to answer what I can answer. I have remembered the first question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, those three questions were questions already asked to you. The first thing is prisoners at Nova Kasaba you saw and your meeting with Mr. -- your encounter with Mr. Mladic in Srebrenica together with Colonel Salapura, and the last thing, the meeting of Mr. Mladic and Kovac at your place. Those were discussed. We are talking about this. And question was -- could you repeat your question just about these three incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Bajagic, what I'm suggesting to you is you left those three things out of your statement in this case. We can agree on that; right? They're not in your statement, are they? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, don't try to trap me. Don't try to play that I didn't want to say that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic --

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: -- to the Trial Chamber because nobody ever asked me about these photos. Nobody has ever asked me about these photos. Nobody has ever shown them to me. This is the first time I'm being asked about them and shown them. And as for Mr. Mladic and Mr. Tomo Kovac, I did say that they were in my house. I said it the last time I testified. And as for the other two things, you are putting these things to me for the first time, and you are trying to imply that I omitted those things intentionally so that the Trial Chamber wouldn't hear about them and wouldn't know about them, and it is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The question may be asked in this way: Did you tell the Defence the fact that Mr. Kovac and General Mladic met at your place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the Defence, Mr. President? Yes. Yes, I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you told them that you testified in the Kos case; right? In the state court.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we be more precise. What Defence, because the witness has testified in several cases so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you can clarify with the witness later on. I clearly meant Defence in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Bajagic, let's move to something completely different. I want to ask you about your relationship with Mr. Karadzic. Now, in paragraph 28 of your statement, if you have a look at it in front of you there. You can see in paragraph 28 you say that you often visited him if he called you on orders of someone in your unit command. Now, in the Popovic case you were talking about this very same thing, and you said at transcript 32506 in that case: "When he," talking about President Karadzic, "needed to see me or wanted to see me, he would call me, and he would say, 'Can you come over at lunch or dinner?'" So that's the way it worked; right? When he wanted to see you, he would call you and ask you to come up to Pale; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: It happened on a numerous -- number of occasions during the four-year time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: But what I'm specifically asking you, he would give you a call and ask you to come up; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Whenever he needed me, the president invited me to come with a good reason, and I called him when I need to talk to him or when I needed to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You also said in the Popovic case, this is at T32509 in that case, that you mostly talked about personal matters, but that that were some official talks as well. You said it had to do with "some civilian issues regarding our municipality, our area, humanitarian aid, accommodation of refugees, dissentiment among the people, the talks, et cetera." So when you'd go up and see President Karadzic in Pale, you'd brief him about the sentiment of the people in Vlasenica about various issues; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, we discussed those issues as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the interpretation we heard the word "Vlasenica" whereas in the transcript we read "Srebrenica." Line 21. The witness received the interpretation as "Vlasenica." At the same time the transcript reflects that as "Srebrenica."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The transcript reads as Vlasenica. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So an issue affecting the sentiment of people in Vlasenica would be something like the fall of Srebrenica, people leaving Srebrenica, all the prisoners who had been caught, those kind of things; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: It depended on the developments and on the time. There were also such questions and issues discussed. Why are you not more precise? Why don't you mention the day, the month, the year? We actually saw each other all the time throughout the four years of war and even before the war, so you should be more precise with regard to the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I will be. You said it depended on the developments as to what you talked about. The fall of Srebrenica was a hugely significant development, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, significant indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And all of the people leaving Srebrenica on buses that went right through the middle of Vlasenica, that's a significant development, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. But let me add to that that we were all glad, I personally, that Srebrenica had fallen, because they were the source of a lot of sorrow and misfortune for all the Serbian villages, particularly those that bordered on Srebrenica, all the villages around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, maybe I can just ask you then about paragraph 36(a) of your statement where you say you were upset that the Muslims were leaving Srebrenica. 36(a). You say you went up to see the president, President Karadzic, because you were upset that the Muslims were leaving Srebrenica. That's not true, is it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: That's true, but let's separate the civilian population of Srebrenica that had suffered the same way as our Serbian population from their soldiers who were villains. That's what I was sorry about. I was sorry that the long-suffering people still suffered. I could see them passing through in those lorries and in those buses by my house. Since I knew Mr. Karadzic as a God fearing and honest person, I asked him about the destiny of those people. I asked him, Mr. President, what will be the lot of these people? Where are they being taken to? What is going to happen to them?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Don't worry, we'll talk about that meeting at length in a little while. You were talking about the kinds of significant developments that you talked to the president about, and you agreed that the fall of Srebrenica, people leaving buses. Another significant development was all the prisoners, right, that had been captured? You'd seen them at Nova Kasaba. So that's another significant development, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was significant, but I was not in the least interested in them, because they were soldiers, and they were the cause of a lot of plight and sorrow. They killed a lot of Serbs. They plundered and burned villages. Maybe not all of them, but in my eyes they were all villains and criminals. It was supposed to be a demilitarised zone, and they were armed to the tooth. They had more ammunition than we did. Whenever they wanted they entered our territory, and whenever they did that they committed crimes. They killed people. They plundered and burned. In the village of Podravanje, they took one of my own employees, they impaled him and they grilled him on the spit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, that must have been pretty significant then. All these villains had been caught; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know if they were all captured but that is my opinion of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bajagic, the Trial Chamber's heard evidence that the killing of some of those prisoners from Srebrenica in Kravica on 13 July was an open secret almost immediately in Bratunac, and it was known in Skelani the same night, and then some of these prisoners were moved to Zvornik and caused great discontent among the people in Zvornik that those prisoners had been moved there. Now, you're in Vlasenica at the headquarters of the Drina Corps. You're at the centre of the military unit in this area. You must have heard about those killings almost immediately; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, we heard about the killings at Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you heard about that almost straight away, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Please explain. What do you mean by "straight away"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The same day.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: No, on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The following day.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on. Let's talk about 1991. Now, you were involved in arming the Serbs in Vlasenica in 1991, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: No. No. You are not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 30461 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, perhaps I can give you a hard copy to make it easier for you to read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. If our usher could assist Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If you can just take your time and have a read of that and let me know when you're done. Why don't you let me know when you're finished the first page. This is quite a lengthy intercept, so let me know when you get to the bottom of page 1.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I've done reading the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: A moment ago I asked you, "You were involved in arming the Serbs in Vlasenica in 1991," and you said, "No. No. You're not right." So page 1 of the intercept, you're talking to President Karadzic, and you tell him, "About 600 volunteers in two days." President Karadzic says, "Brilliant." And then you say, "They have all been clothed and armed." So that's you talking about arming the Serbs in Vlasenica in 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: On page 1 it doesn't say that they were clothed and armed, but these are not volunteers. That's what we call them. They were soldiers who responded to the mobilisation call. At that time, the Army of Yugoslavia still existed and the command was very close by in Han Pijesak. Mobilisation was carried out and people responded as volunteers. That's how we referred to them, volunteers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably he needs to read the second page as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Why don't you read the second and third pages, Mr. Bajagic. If you go over the page. Read page 2.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: One page is missing here. There's page 2, and then there's page 4. The pages are not in order. I'm missing a page here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Why don't you look at the screen in front of you then. Can you read that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: It's not easy. A page is missing here. You can't have the word "excellent" here and then the following entry says, "Tomorrow we are going to." So there's no sequence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Our usher will bring you a new set of intercept. Could you take a look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's five pages long. If it were more convenient, we could break and let Mr. Bajagic read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Bajagic, we'll have a break now for 45 minutes, and during the break you may read the intercept so you can answer the question about it. We will have a break for 50 minutes and resume at quarter past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that the Defence was not planning to call the next witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the Defence wished that tomorrow we start at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be done. Yes, please continue, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, you've had an opportunity to read the intercept over lunch?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: At the top of the second page in B/C/S you say -- you're talking about the volunteers. They have all been clothed and armed. That's you talking about arming Serb volunteers, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, I conveyed this to Mr. President during the conversation, that they were clothed and armed, and we used to call them volunteers because they responded to mobilisation voluntarily, which had been conducted by the then draft office, and these were call-up papers sent by the Yugoslav People's Army. As for the fact that I said they were clothed and armed that meant that the Yugoslav Army provided clothes and arms for them because they were the ones who mobilised them. Where could we find arms to arm 600 people and to clothe them?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, go on to page 2 in the English, the bottom of page 2 in your document, you say to President Karadzic: Seeing as the party has done it all. And then if we go over to page 3 in the English, 4 in the B/C/S, we see President Karadzic say: They helped the army up there. The party helped the army form a volunteers detachment. The party is the SDS, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, can I first answer the question and then the question relating to everything was completed by the party, because you haven't read until the very end. The party completed this, but that means that we were preparing a feast to celebrate such a successful response by people to mobilisation, so we wanted to celebrate that. So the party and the local people prepared all the food, drink, and orchestras, and this is what the party was involved in organising, and there were also participation in that by some companies and local farmers who provided food in order for the feast to be as lavish as possible. That's one thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, let me stop you there. Let me stop you there. Go to page 4 in your copy, and you see the President saying: The party helped the army to form a volunteers detachment. They're not talking about refreshments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we see the passage in English as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: It's page 3 in English, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't find it. Radovan, what is he saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: It's the big paragraph in the fifth box down, and you can see President Karadzic says to someone else: The party helped the army form a volunteers detachment. They're not talking about the party helped prepare a feast. They're talking about the party helped prepare or helped form a volunteers detachment.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't find it. Can you please point it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you look at the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, but where is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you see it now where President Karadzic says: The party helped the army to form a volunteers detachment. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Under the command of the Yugoslav People's Army. Is that it? It's further on in this passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: No. It's right after where it says: Karadzic is talking to Nikola in the office. The very next sentence is: They helped the army up there. The party helped the army to form a volunteers detachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The passage you referred to follows after that. They were under the JNA command. They were clothed. They were in JNA uniform. Very well, what is your question Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: My question was very simple, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The party --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's put a pause. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: In this conversation where both you and President Karadzic are talking about the party. You are talking about the SDS, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, the SDS party. But I did not give an answer to your question. You are insisting on this being done by the party. Let me tell you, the direct cause for this mobilisation and this response was something that indicated to us that something was in the offing, because the SDA promotion of that party took place in 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, probably you spoke a bit too fast for the interpreters. Could you repeat, "The direct cause for this mobilisation ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reason for carrying out mobilisation, and we actually asked for it, was occasioned by fear among Serbs in the district of Vlasenica, because the first promotion of the SDA party for Bosnia-Herzegovina took place in Vlasenica. This is something that caused concern amongst us, the fact that it took place in Vlasenica instead of Sarajevo. Knowing what happened to Serbs in 1941 in the Vlasenica district we surmise that something bad was in the making and it turned out to be true. From the 6th of April, 1941, until the 22nd June, 1946 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, can I stop you there. My question was simply that the reference to the party was the SDS, and you said yes; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I tender this, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the intercept is already in evidence as Exhibit D1653.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back to 1995, 12th of July. If I can play P4201 and the transcript is P4202. This is part 2 of the Srebrenica trial video, and we're starting at time-code 39 minutes and 2 seconds?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters have difficulty finding the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please turn the volume down a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the Prosecutor give us the reference where the transcript starts from, because we have full text, the whole page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if we can start from the beginning. I didn't understand a thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll do so, but if -- Mr. Mitchell, could you give the reference to the interpreters. They have the whole book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, the transcript's in the trial video book at ERN 07047875. That's where we are starting from.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Since we don't have the transcript, we're going to read from the screen: "[Voiceover] Trust me, I only look towards our church inspiring some wish because I grew up there, and believe me in my document it says Easter 1995. And it says Vlasenica. Even officially to score differently now documents but I wrote it down in my documents that this is Easter."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It stopped now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I just want to ask you a couple of questions. That's, in the middle of the screen, General Zivanovic; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And can you tell us what this occasion is?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: That's the date of St. Peter and Paul. It is celebrated by our church in Vlasenica and also the patron saint of the SDS party, and this is me preparing a lunch, as I do every year in the church for selected guests.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And that's you, we can see, just on the right-hand side of the screen about halfway up; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Now I can't hear you. Can you please turn the volume up now and can you repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We can see you in this shot, can't we, just half of you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Who do you see?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: No, I don't see myself here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We'll keep playing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] And I guess our enemies wanted it to be higher than the church and therefore they took down half of our bell."

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You can see yourself there now; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: That's at 40 minutes and 7 seconds. We'll keep playing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] I guess our enemies wanted to make it higher than the church, to make the minaret higher. However, [indiscernible] this morning, General has this famous mosque been finished. I told him I think that they finished it this morning. That's what I said, finished this morning. Well, let me tell you some more. The town as such was not -- as such was not crowded with residents as they sold over Motorola. No, no, no. It was not like that. They had fantastic weaponry in Motorolas and scared, gullible Serbs. It is best to listen to the Turks as little as possible and one should not listen to some of the less good Serbs. Simply take the sword in your hand and go ahead. Our army started out powerfully. Yesterday, Yuni [phoen] forces were introduced from the police force in Bratunac towards Potocari. One wing of our army went towards Viogor. Viogor is the crest of the hills towards Milici, Srebrenica and so. God willing, we will get to Derventa from Srebrenica. That is our task. Yesterday at dusk -- no, from Milici to Derventa. From Srebrenica to Derventa. Yes, from Srebrenica to Derventa. Let me tell you that with yesterday's task any organised Muslim life to the left of Jadar ceased to exist."

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: All right. Before I ask you a question, I want to jump to the very end of this speech and if we can play 65 ter 40369A, and this clip starts at 1 minute -- sorry, 1 hour and 24 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: All right. So we've just seen the commander of the Drina Corps, General Zivanovic, giving a speech about organised Muslim life to the left of Jadar ceased existing at dusk the previous day, 11 July, and you also heard him talking about flattening at least one or possibly two mosques. Mr. -- Mr. Bajagic, why midday on 12 July when the women, children, and elderly population of Srebrenica is still in Potocari is the commander of the Drina Corps talking about blowing up a mosque and the end of organised life?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know how Zivanovic could have said something like this. As far as I know, he never went to Srebrenica, and he did not lead the action in Srebrenica. It was led by Krstic. I didn't see any demolished mosques, and I didn't see the belfry in Srebrenica demolished. The whole church was devastated, and everything inside was desecrated, but as far as I remember, the belfry remained intact, but he was bragging about this. That's what I think, because the people from the top leadership of command wanted to remove him, and since he delivered this speech as he did, maybe they gave up on the idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, you know that --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript. In line 9, the witness said that he wasn't in Srebrenica, Zivanovic, not himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then if you want to check, it's in line 9, it refers to Zivanovic. "I never went to Srebrenica" should read "He never went to Srebrenica." And in lines 14 and 15 it says, "They gave up on the idea." Instead, the witness says "Half of it was untrue." He never spoke about giving up on the idea. He stated that whatever Zivanovic said, half of it was untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bajagic, the bit about flattening the mosque was true, wasn't it? You know that the mosque in Srebrenica had its minaret flattened after the VRS took the town; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Later on I saw it myself, but I didn't see it at the time. Whether it happened on the same day or the next day, I didn't see it then. I didn't say it wasn't flattened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, just one more thing on this video. Paragraph 36(a) of your statement, you said that you were upset that the Muslims were leaving Srebrenica, and yet we saw you at a speech with General Zivanovic talking about the end of organised life and flattening a mosque. And you toasted him at the end of that speech. You weren't upset about those Muslims leaving at all, were you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, it's a celebration. I'm not going to cry when -- are celebrating. You don't know what the Serbs' customs are. He delivered a toast, and it is a duty of a host to return a toast and to greet his guests. So you cannot make such judgements about me saying that I wasn't upset at all simply based on the fact that I raised a glass to him. Please don't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I tender that last little clip, 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was it not already in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: No, it wasn't, Mr. President. It's the very end of General Zivanovic's speech, but we didn't include that in the trial video compilation, and it was done a couple of years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was the 65 ter number for that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could identify the time-frame later on of what we saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We saw on that video time-codes 1 hour, 24 minutes and 0 seconds through to 1 hour 24 minutes and 31 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6442, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I have Exhibit P2241 in e-court, and it's page 91 in both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I want to turn now, Mr. Bajagic, to your meeting with President Karadzic in the early morning hours of 15 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I understand my hour and a half is almost up. I have two subjects I'd like to cover with the witness. One is this meeting, and one is another meeting at the Bratunac Brigade, and I think it will probably take me another 45, 50 minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please try to conclude in half an hour, please, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, you can see on the left-hand side of the screen this is President Karadzic's appointment diary, the entry for 14 July 1995, and you can see your name there twice; is that right? The first entry says, "Call Zvonko Bajagic," and the second entry says "Zvonko Bajagic" with a time-code after it. Can you see both of them?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I can only see one of the entries at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The "call Zvonko Bajagic" is four entries up from the bottom, and the meet is the very last entry on the page.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Now, earlier you agreed that, you know, when President Karadzic wanted to see you it was normal for him to call you and ask you to come up to Pale, and we've got evidence from one of President Karadzic's secretaries about how -- how this diary worked, and her statement is P4358. At paragraph 33 she explains that the secretaries would schedule an activity for President Karadzic by putting a minus sign, and once that activity had occurred, that would convert the minus sign to a plus sign. So we can see a plus sign next to the entry "call Zvonko Bajagic," which means that they scheduled a call and then the call was completed. So isn't it true that President Karadzic called you and asked you to come up to Pale on the evening of 14 July?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the date. I did visit the president. Was it on the 13th, 14th, 15th, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Right. But putting aside the date --

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I think it is more likely that it was on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. But my question was: He called you, as it says in the book -- or it indicates in the book he called you and asked you to come up to Pale; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I don't recall him calling me. I know that I went to Pale. I went to see the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. And earlier I asked you about your official VRS car, the Golf. You took this car to see the president on that visit, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, I probably did. I don't remember which car I took.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mitchell, shall we clarify this. The diary agenda we see before us is dated 14th of July, but when Mr. Zvonko Bajagic met Mr. Karadzic was past midnight, so that's 15th, early in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The very early morning hours of 15 July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So Mr. Bajagic's memory is correct. Maybe it's night of 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Right. I want to ask you about the length of this meeting, Mr. Bajagic. In paragraph 36 of your statement, you say that you and President Karadzic just ran into each other in the hallway. You had a short exchange and then he did not talk to me again, just passed me and went off. Now, that's not true, is it? You met with the president, as it says in his appointment book, for 50 minutes.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know if it was me saying that or that somebody misrecorded that we came across each other in the hallway. I recall that we went into the office and had a short conversation. As for what you say that I was there for an hour, I probably was, because normally after my conversation with the president, a friend and a relative of mine were members of president's security detail. So I would normally go and have a cup of coffee or a shot of rakija with them, and I probably did stay on a bit further talking to Batko Kovacevic and who else was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: This is the president's appointment diary. His secretary told us, this is again page 30 -- paragraph 33 of her statement, P4358, that the first number -- sorry, in the brackets you can see two numbers. The first number shows a time when the guest entered the president's office. The second number is the time when the guest left the president's office. So we can see you going into the president's office at 12.35, and you exiting the president's office at 1.25; right? That's 50 minutes.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Look, where the secretary's desk is is a connecting room. There was a door there to one office and to two or three offices, perhaps, and it was in that other room that I continued socialising with my acquaintances, and so it was probably only after that second conversation that I went through the room where the secretary's desk was, and then she noted down that particular time as the time that I left the president's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So the secretary --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript. Nothing is properly reflected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, if there's -- if there's a substantive transcript correction --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let us hear it. Let us hear from him. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said that when you pass the room which is in between, which is where the secretary's desk is, when you enter the office of the president, that's where there is a complex of room beyond, and that wasn't reflected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So it's your evidence that the secretary of the president of the republic got this wrong. It was just a mistake in his appointment diary.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: The error is in the fact that you believe that I spent the entire time with the president. I wasn't. I was there for a short time, but then I was in another office with that other person that I mentioned. I talked to him. I was seated there, and these fellows there were offering refreshments. So when I got out of that office, she must have recorded that time when I left one of the offices there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, the secretaries testified indeed that during the time-frame noted here the president may have done something else, meeting something -- somebody else, receiving some telephone calls, but at this time-frame, half past 12.00 at midnight, there was no other guest. It was only you. Was it not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if there was anybody else. I was there, but I was there for a short time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, your -- your testimony today has given us a much fuller picture of exactly who you'd been meeting with on the 13th of July, your knowledge of the Srebrenica prisoners, your knowledge of the Kravica killings, your knowledge of the meeting between General Mladic and Tomo Kovac, all of which you had when you met with President Karadzic in the early morning hours of 15 July. Now, I want to ask you about that, but let me just put one more thing to you. If I can have 65 ter 25350 in e-court, page 43. This is an interview with -- between the Office of the Prosecutor and Tomo Kovac. It's only in English. Mr. Kovac is being asked about reporting to President Karadzic at this time, and he was asked the question about halfway down the page: "So let me get this straight. Is the reason that you are saying that you did not discuss or protest to the president what was happening with the army killing people because you thought he already knew from all these other sources?" And then Tomo Kovac said: "This is crystal clear because he had Bajagic who knew everything. He had Deronjic. He received all the information that he needed from them. He had the entire nomenclature there, people who knew everything and who controlled everything." Now, Mr. Bajagic, it's our position that Tomo Kovac isn't being a hundred per cent truthful about his involvement in the murder of the Srebrenica prisoners, but he was telling the truth about you; right? You did go up there and tell everything to President Karadzic that you knew at the time, all of the significant developments that we talked about earlier.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: First let me correct you. You say that I knew everything. A moment ago you also said and made comments about the prisoners in Srebrenica. I didn't know that, and I didn't say that. I said that I saw them at the pitch in Nova Kasaba and that it was on the following day that I heard about the liquidation in Kravica. As for Tomo saying that I knew everything and that I should be asked about everything and that I and this other Deronjic are reporting about everything, well, it depends -- well, he -- on what he was telling the president. So me as an infantryman with all the superiors above me, how would I be able to know everything? You say that I knew everything. That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, I didn't say you knew everything. I said you told the president everything that you knew at the time, and what you knew at the time included that lots of prisoners had been captured. You saw them at Nova Kasaba, and you said that you knew about the Kravica killings on the 14th of July. You met with the president in the early morning hours of 15 July. So you knew about prisoners, and you knew about killings at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Have a look at that date again. I wasn't clear enough. It was the 14th in the morning and not the 15th in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the night of 14th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in the evening. It was the dawn of the 14th, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to see the agenda again? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. I'd like to see the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: It's P2241, page 91.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And if we need to do this, Mr. Bajagic, we'll look at your vehicle log, too, if that would assist. Isn't it true --

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: First show me what I asked for and then later we can look at the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Collapse the English this time. The upper part is 13th of July. 13th of July ends at 22.10 or 22.15, and the bottom part, last half, is 14th of July and starts from 6.00 in the evening and ends at 1.35 or 25 the next day. Now, do you follow, Mr. Bajagic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This happened on the morning of the 14th and so based on what you're saying, this would have been the 15th. 00.35 to 01.25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So 15th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my recollect it was on the 14th, in the morning. The 14th, in the morning. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But this agenda says it's the 15th morning. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember that it was late in the evening on the 13th that I set out and that it happened on the morning of the 14th. That's how I remember.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript. What the witness said probably wasn't [In English] "I remember." It should rather be translated "It is in my mind."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. There's not much difference. Would you like to show the vehicle log to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We can look at the vehicle log, Mr. President. It's 65 ter 25354.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We have the original here which we can show you, Mr. Bajagic, if that would help. And you'll see two entries there that I want you to focus on, one on the 14th of July which says Vlasenica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you wait until we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let's start with the front page. You can see your name on the front page; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And we can see registration number P7105. That's the same car that we were talking about earlier this morning that you were assigned in 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. If we go to the next page, you'll see two trips. Now, you just told us that it was your recollection that you set out late in the evening of the 13th. Now, you'll agree that there's nothing --

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- on the 13th of July that mentions a trip to Pale; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: But it does mention a trip to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And then we can see two entries: One on the 14th that says Vlasenica, Pal -- Vlasenica, Loko, and one on the 15th that says Vlasenica, Milici, Pale, Vlasenica, Loko. And one of these two trips has been entered either on the late night of the 14th, the early morning of the 15th and that is your trip to see the president; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: You see on this first travel order it says the 12th, one of these. It doesn't have the 13th. And then the other one has the 13th, Vlasenica, Srebrenica. The 14th, Vlasenica, Pale. This was enter into the order. But you see the number of kilometres. From me [as interpreted] to Pale it's 95 kilometres one way. So if I had the intention of going to Pale on the 14th, and I didn't, then this is the number of kilometres that were travelled along a different route. So this confirms it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. But you agree you did go and see the president in Pale, right, at some point? So the trip actually happened.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. And to my recollection, it was the 13th in the evening and the night onto the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Right. But you agree the only two entries there -- there's 14th and 15th mention trips to Pale. There's nothing on the 13th; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can see that there is no mention of it. But you see, the 15th, if there was also the intention to go to Pale, it says 130 kilometres, Pale, Vlasenica. Two ways is 190 kilometres there and back, only that, excluding any driving that I might have done on some of the side roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Right. So what you're saying now is to the best of your recollection this happened on the 13th, right? That's what you're saying now.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Late in the evening. Late.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Right. Let me read you what you said in paragraph 36 of your statement when you're talking about your trip to Srebrenica on the 13th and you say: I don't recall whether it was that day or the next day after returning from Srebrenica that I went to Pale. However, I think it was the next day. That's in your statement.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, here it remains vague as well. I don't remember if I was. Did I? Did I not? I think it was the next day. When I'm racking my brains I think that it was Wednesday evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Right. But there's nothing vague about the appointment diary, is there? The president's appointment diary clearly says the last entry of the day, Zvonko Bajagic, 12.35 to 1.25 in the morning, 50 minutes; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I said what I think on the matter, and there's no need for you to ring me further on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me tell you our position on what happened at that meeting. President Karadzic called you, as we see in the appointment diary, and he asked you to come up to Pale for a meeting. So you drove up to Pale, you met with the President for 50 minutes in the middle of the night. This meeting was so urgent it couldn't wait until the morning. It wasn't something you wanted to talk about over the phone. During this 50 minutes with the president, you talked to him about all the significant developments that had been going on in the last -- at least the last couple of days, the meeting with General Mladic and Tomo Kovac at your house, your meetings with General Mladic, Colonel Salapura, the prisoners you saw at Nova Kasaba, the killings that had been going on at Kravica that you knew about by the morning of 15 July, and you went up there to tell him about the sentiment of the people of Vlasenica, about all of these things that had been going on, the fall of Srebrenica, the prisoners, the capture of those villains that you told us about, the villains and criminals --

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let me finish.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Oh my dear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The capture of those villains and criminals that you told us about that had caused you so much misery over the last three years. These are the significant developments that you went up to talk to him about; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: That's what you say as if you were there with me in the office. How should you know what I was saying there. That's not true. Don't tell me that I had a meeting with Salapura and the general. I was in Srebrenica. I came across them in front of that house, and I went into the house with them, had a look and then I went on my way. I didn't have a meeting either with Salapura or with Mladic in Srebrenica. As for President Radovan, I know full well what I told him, as if I was Salapura, that's how you're treating me, and not Zvonko Bajagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think my time's almost up. There is one other last area that's about the date of a meeting at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters and about the credibility of Mr. Bajagic's testimony in the Popovic case on that. It's testimony that he gave about a meeting related to Srebrenica. It's exactly what he's testifying about here, and I think his credibility on that issue is going to be relevant to Your Honours determining the credibility of his evidence here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just add, we have to leave some time for redirect. It's taken a lot more time and it's been relatively slow, so I think we have to consider the time that he's already used and to make sure that Dr. Karadzic has an adequate time to do redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was wondering whether that issue will be relevant to this case. Can we not skip it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, we think -- it's our position it's a credibility issue in this case. He came to testify about the date of a meeting on behalf of one of the accused in the Srebrenica operation. He's now come to testify about another meeting. This time the issue isn't the date, it's the content of the meeting and so it's purely credibility, but given that he's testifying about a meeting in this period, I think it's important that Your Honours hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Mitchell, how much time would you want? Could you give us some idea at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I sincerely hope it would be 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Fifteen minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I hope that would be all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the circumstances, we'll allow you to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, can you look at your statement, paragraphs 29 to 32, where you describe a meeting at the Bratunac Brigade on -- that you say took place on 11 July. Now when you testified in the Popovic case you were called by Vinko Pandurevic for the sole purpose of putting Vinko Pandurevic at this meeting that both you and Pandurevic said happened on 11 July; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I was not at any meetings and I was not called by Pandurevic. Where did you get that information from? I didn't say that. In the evening on the 11th I went to the command of the Bratunac Brigade. That's what happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. You say the date was on the 11th; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: In the evening on the 11th I was at the command of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Right. And what you told the Popovic Trial Chamber is the reason why you recall that this meeting was on 11th July was because 11th July was a fasting day when you had to eat fish. Your testimony was that on 12 July, it was a feast day where you ate meat, and you even talked about in your testimony that the preparations for suckling pig and lamb that you were going to serve on the 12th of July. And so you said because you served fish at the Bratunac Brigade, the meeting had to happened on the 11th of July. Have I summarised that accurately?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I took food to treat them in the evening. It was a -- a lean dinner. That was on the evening of St. Peter's Day, and we were fasting. St. Peter's Day was on the following day. I don't know if it was Wednesday or Friday. I don't know but in our parts we fast on both Wednesday and Friday. So on the following day I served fish to those who wanted fish. At the same time, we grilled a lamb, and a suckling pig to those who wanted to eat meat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, your testimony in the Popovic case was crystal clear. You served fish on the 11th and you served meat and the 12th, and that's why you said the meeting was on the 11th. It was the thing that tied your recollection to the 11th, the serving of fish; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I was the one who served fish? I was not the one who was served fish. Colonel Kacanovic asked me if I could take dinner to the building of the brigade command. He asked me if I had any surplus fish to take there. He asked me if I needed a car, and I said yes, I do have surplus of food. It was no fat food. I came to the brigade command. I spent there only a short period of time in the corridor. I saw General Mladic as well as Krstic and Vinko Pandurevic and some other people whom I can't remember as I sit here today, and then I returned home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. But now you're saying you served fish on both days, the 11th and the 12th; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a lot of fish. A friend from [indiscernible] had brought a fish. There was a lot of it. There were people who had fish even on the 12th, whereas I at the same time prepared some pork and some lamb. For example, Vladika Vasilje he didn't want to eat meat. He stuck to the fish. That's as much as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: However, why does it matter to you whether they had fish or meat? Why do you care?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, we've got your vehicle log up on the screen there. You would agree with me there's not a trip to Bratunac on either the 11th or 12th of July, is there?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: And where doesn't it say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Have a look at the vehicle log.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, if it doesn't say so here, that doesn't necessarily mean that I didn't go there. This is not a yardstick by which you had to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So you just left this trip out of the vehicle log?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, if it's not here, that means I didn't enter that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. One final thing. Now, you've told us that you saw Vinko Pandurevic. Are you absolutely certain that you saw Vinko Pandurevic at that meeting? Is that your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I am not saying that that was a meeting. They were all there at the meeting. Most probably they had a meeting, but I saw Vinko. I claimed that then. I claim it still. I told you that Vinko is hard to miss wherever he appears. He is a guy from Romanija, but there is nobody else on Mount Romanija who is freckled and has fiar hair. He is big, he is sturdy, but he is the only fair-haired person with freckles from Mount Romanija. Actually, he is more red haired than fair haired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. My point simply was you saw Vinko Pandurevic that night. You're absolutely certain?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I confirm this to you for the third time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let's look at 65 ter 25280.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you tender that vehicle log?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, please Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6443, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: What I'm bringing up here, Mr. Bajagic, is your testimony in the Kos case in the state court in 2011. It's only in English so I'll have to read it to you. If we can go to page 2 we see that you took an oath to speak the whole truth and not conceal anything that's known to you. And on page 1 the Judge specifically cautioned you that you mustn't withhold anything because perjury constitute a criminal offence. If we go to page 15 and the second half of the page one of the lawyers says to you: The night before St. Peter's Day when you came to the command of the Bratunac Brigade who did you -- you speak to about who you saw there. And you said apart from Ratko Mladic you saw Radislav Krstic and Vinko Pandurevic and you say: That I saw Vinko? The lawyer says: Yes. On the 11th? And the lawyer says to you: On the 12th I think or the 11th. And you say, your first answer: I didn't see Vinko on the 11th. Now, if we go over the page the Defence lawyer shows you your statement from the Popovic case and says: Let me refresh your recollection and shows you the statement, and then in line 15 you say: On the 11th in the evening hours I can't recall, and then line 20 you say I either made a mistake and said he was not there but I think he wasn't there. So today you're absolutely certain that he was there. Two years ago he wasn't there, "I don't recall," and, "I don't think he was there."

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: No. There was a confusion there. They were asking me about the 12th, whether I saw Vinko on the 12th, and I didn't see him on the 12th. There may be a confusion with the dates. And in the evening on the 11th I did see Vinko. I did not see him only the 12th. There must be a mistake there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can we go back just one page. Mr. Bajagic, your first answer, the very first answer you gave, there's no confusion about the 12th, these are your words: I didn't see Vinko on the 11th. Crystal clear.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: If I said that, I made a mistake. I swore before God more than I did before you. I saw him on the 11th. They asked me about the 12th, whether I saw Vinko on the 12th, and I said I did not. I didn't go to Srebrenica on the 12th. That whole day was my holiday. From that morning on the 12th to that evening on the 12th which was St. Peter's Day I had guests. So I did see Vinko on the 11th, but I didn't see him on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If Mr. Bajagic provides as short answers to me as he did to the Prosecutor, I believe that I will be able to finish today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're talking about this, tell the Trial Chamber would a host ever leave his home on his own religious holiday?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I've never heard of anybody leaving his home on his religious holiday, on his main religious holiday. I didn't do that ever, nor did I ever hear of anybody else who did it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at P6443. And the document that we saw before the last one. The one before last.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what is the first date on this document?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: The 8th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And can we now look at the other page? I believe that it was either the next page or page 4. What page was that? What page did we see before? Can the Serbian version be zoomed in? What's the first date that appears here?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: The 22nd of July, and then the 22nd of June, and then this is crossed out. The 22nd of June is crossed out, and what follows is the 23rd of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the month of June or the month of July in the first row?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: It's the month of June. In one place 6 has been altered into 7, I believe, and again there -- there are -- there is the month of June three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Pale, did you arrive only to see me or did you have any other things to do in Pale? Did you visit anybody else?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't come to Pale only because of you. I didn't only come to visit you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During your visit to my office, did we sit down? Did we chat sitting down?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: It was a very brief encounter. I don't know whether you remember what I asked you on that occasion. I asked you about the transport of the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did we discuss anything else?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At that point in time did you know what had happened in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: No, I only learnt about that the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you learn that on the following day after you had visited me or after that had happened?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: One day after I visited you. After I visited you, the following day I learnt about Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 59 you were interrupted where you were saying that from 20th April to June 1994 people were killed. Can you tell in one sentence who was killed?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: The most renowned Serbian intellectuals, teachers, one or two men from every village, and nine priests from the diocese, and also the Jews but one were killed. My grandfather himself was killed on the Easter of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who killed him?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Those people will -- killed by Muslims from Vlasenica. At the top of that organisation was Rasim Begovic who sported a Karadjordje star because he was a volunteer at Salon. After 1945 he was convicted and executed in Vlasenica, and that execution was carried out by Med Oberga [phoen] who killed him with a mullet. Perhaps you don't know that his grandchild, Jusuf Dautovic, who was an engineer, he was the head of the HOS. We didn't know that and we were all surprised to learn that there was an HOS organisation in a place where there -- where there were no Croats or Catholics. We found on his body a list of those Serbs who had to be killed on Easter Friday. The chief at the time, Rade Bjelanovic, showed me that and I have never heard that anybody has mentioned this document. It seems that nobody's interested in that. There were 200 of us on that list. I was number 3. Number 1 was Dr. Milorad Lukic, and number 2 was priest Milorad Golijan. I was number 3 on at that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us when that list was found on the grandson of that person who was the protagonist of 1941?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: It was on the 21st or the 22nd of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The event when somebody was impaled and grilled he was your employee, I believe. Was that something that you perceived as a drastic moment?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, everybody who has a heart and soul has to feel something. They were not human beings. They were beasts those people who could do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How -- how does it arise from the cross of Mr. Mitchell? What's the relevance?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevance is based on Mr. Mitchell's thesis about drastic events that are missing from the statement. And now my next question to the gentleman would be to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Move on to another topic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, were you asked questions and providing answers or did you yourself suggest what the substance of your statement should be? If anybody should ask you about something, would your -- would you be answering in response to that or would you volunteer information?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Would you repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you yourself formulate the statement or did you answer questions?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I was answering questions. I wasn't writing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And unless somebody puts a question to you on a subject, would you yourself suddenly -- would it come to your mind to start speaking about that topic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, I was speaking about matters that I was being asked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A question was put to you about whether you had said anything to the Defence. How many Defence teams did you talk to?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, I spoke to the Defence team in the Popovic case and to the -- your Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who did you testify for in Bosnia? Was it for the Defence or --

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, it was for Kos. It was Dusko Tomic, the lawyer who placed me on the witness list without even consulting me. I merely received a summons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was also for the Defence; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, I suppose so, for this person Kos. He was in that case. He even wanted to extend this, but the lady judge wouldn't agree. He was shifting some blame onto you and to a bishop, and he was trying to add something, but the president of the chamber interrupted him and did not allow him to speak on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us who was it from my Defence team who spoke to you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Luka from Bratunac. What's his last name. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you arrived in The Hague for the proofing, did you speak about this meeting with Mladic and Kovac on the 12th and the 13th? When was it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Sorry, who did I speak to about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To my Defence team. Did you speak to him about it? Did you tell them this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just a second. Mr. Bajagic, if you could excuse yourself for a moment. We have something to discuss in your absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, that was inexcusable, the attempting to suggest to the witness that the meeting with Mladic and Kovac happened on the 12th or the 13th. It's crystal clear that that meeting happened in the late afternoon of 13th July.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said on the 12th or the 13th. I wasn't sure about it. But that's not the point when the meeting was. Rather, who did he tell this to without it having ended up in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, we -- first thing, we've got a draft statement. The statement had additional information added to it and Mr. Bajagic arrived here. So he's clearly met with people other than Luka in Bratunac. Second thing is the Defence had, was disclosed to them the transcripts in the Kos case and just -- it was either last week or the week before we got the Defence statement from the Kos case and disclosed it which contains the same information. It's a short, basically a one-page statement which talks about Nova Kasaba, the meeting between Mladic and Kovac. It doesn't mention his meeting with Mladic and Salapura, but it's got the two things, Nova Kasaba, lots of prisoners. It's got the Mladic-Kovac meeting. They've got both the transcript and a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Shall we continue then? We'll bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at the intercept that was shown to you, and I think it was D1653. Mr. Bajagic, can you tell the Chamber what sort of a position the SDS had vis-a-vis the response to the call-up, and which was that of the SDA in respect of Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, the response to the call-up was multi-ethnic. The Muslims responded to it as well. They were there for a couple of days, and then one night they all left, and we realised that they had been ordered by the SDA to withdraw. Later on they withdrew all the soldiers from the Yugoslav Army as well. They all went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you in the SDS in Vlasenica have your paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't have that. The SDA did. We did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the next page. Can you tell the Chamber who is General Djurdjevac?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: He was the commander of the Sarajevo Corps. Since the military post of Han Pijesak came under the command of the Sarajevo Corps, we expressed our wish for General Djurdjevac to join us for this occasion, to spend the day with us there. He was a general of the Yugoslav People's Army at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the two next pages. You were shown that large paragraph. That was page 4. Can you have a look there. My intervention, which is quite long, where I suggest that Biljana Plavsic should come because she's a woman and a representative of the official authority. Can you tell us did the party want to interfere? Did it want to impose itself on military matters either during the JNA or later the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: No. The party did not meddle. It did not interfere with the affairs of the army. However, we did want you to come. It was our special wish. And the army expressed that wish as well. Everybody was telling me it would really be a good thing if Radovan came, because mobilisation was organised very swiftly out of fear, and as a result the people in the area felt safe, that 1941 would not happen all over again simply because they had that unit there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bajagic, for coming here to testify. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, just one thing. Perhaps the witness should take his headphones off for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, at page 53 today, lines 20 to 23, it was crystal clear that Mr. Bajagic said that he knew about the killings at Kravica the following day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm coming to that. Could you leave it there? I was about to raise that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Oh, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can come back after I ask some supplemental questions if I do not deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic. Body language is universal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wanted to be clear about what you said. We talked about the killing at the Kravica warehouse. You remember that. And you testified that you came to know about the killing on the next day.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we know now the killing took place on the 13th of July, so we can conclude, can't we, that you came to know about the killing on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: 14th or the 15th. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You unequivocally say that on the following day you came to know -- you heard about the killing the following day. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, the next day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the time when you met Mr. Karadzic was on the night, late night of 14th, we can conclude that you knew about or you heard about the Kravica warehouse killing at that time, can't we?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what you conclude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we take a look at the agenda again. Can you upload P2242. Mr. Karadzic's secretary's agenda. My understanding is we had a hard book, a hard copy of it, but we shall do with the e-court. It's page 91, but shall we begin with page 89. We'll just deal with the B/C/S version, collapsing the English version. Can you zoom in further. So this is 10th of July. Do you see that, Mr. Bajagic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: During the course of proceeding Dr. Karadzic said his biorhythm, he's an afternoon person. His agenda starts at 2.00 in the afternoon on the 10th of July and ends late night, almost 3.00 the next morning. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So this is 10th of July. Can you we see the next page. So up -- so we can conclude that upper part is now 12th of July. It starts at 2.00 in the afternoon and ends at 10.55 at night. Or 11th of July. I'm sorry. And then 12th of July starts at 1.00 - and shall we go down - and concludes at 6.00 in the -- in the evening. That's the 12th. Okay? Shall we go back to the next page. Now we come to the 13th. It starts at 4.25 and ends at 22.15, 10.15. And the bottom part relates to 14th of July, which starts at 6.00 and ends 1.45 or 25 next -- the next morning, which is 15th, early in the morning, or night of 14th. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, according to the records here, I can see that that's the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I'd like to ask you once again for the last time, according to the agenda -- to this agenda, it was night of 14th that you met Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: What lingers in my memory is that it was between the 13th and the 14th, and it does read the 14th here, and I said it was very short. Radovan was a bit nervous. When I mentioned the people, who was moving out, what they were doing, he told me, Zvonko, mind your own business and that is the extent of it. He said, What do you care. And so I stayed on with these fellows having a drink with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I have one final question for you. When you talked about the civilian population or prisoners from Srebrenica, civilian population, you said this, it's page 52 of today's transcript: "That's what I was sorry about. I was sorry that long-suffering people still suffered. I could see them passing through in those lorries and in those buses by my house.
